utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. My name is Jan Wubben, senior trial attorney for the Prosecution together with Ms. Joanne Richardson, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to your team. Appearances for the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends of the Prosecution. I am Vasvija Vidovic, and together with John Jones I represent Mr. Oric. Together with us are Jasmina Cosic, our legal assistant, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Vidovic, and good morning to you and to the rest of your team. We have got a lot to do this morning. And as I explained yesterday we will start with an expose of the guidelines that this Trial Chamber after due consultation amongst ourselves decided to make known to you. And these guidelines relate essentially to matters of evidence and procedure but also they relate to the conduct that each person present in this room is expected to -- in this courtroom is expected to adhere to. What I will be saying now will be handed down to you subsequently, probably early next week, in writing. In other words, this is the oral decision that we are handing down today. It will be followed by a written version which will reflect what I will be saying in perhaps a little bit more detail and in a more refined manner. Let me first explain to you what this Trial Chamber understands by the term of evidence. This Trial Chamber takes evidence to mean all that information which will be put before us with a view to proving the facts in issue, and we consider such evidence to take different forms. One of the most important forms is testimony, testimony which we can receive viva voce or under some other provision of the rules. Evidence can also take the form of documents which are not tendered in evidence as such as exhibits but they are produced for the inspection of the Trial Chamber. Then we have real evidence, and by real evidence we mean exhibits and other material objects. And last but not least, even though we have got very few of those on the face of it, what we would describe as admissions of fact. But as you both know, there are very few matters on which there is agreement between the parties. In its exercise of deciding on the admissibility of evidence, which is an ongoing and will remain as an ongoing process throughout the entire trial, the Trial Chamber will divide it under categories. Category one would be direct and indirect evidence; category two will be original and hearsay evidence; category three primary and secondary evidence; and last but not least circumstantial evidence. I will be dealing with these categories as we go along. But let me say at the very outset that hearsay and circumstantial evidence will be considered as indirect evidence with the understanding that indirect evidence may at times be as much evidence as direct evidence. With regard to primary and secondary evidence, although the Trial Chamber's -- in the Trial Chamber's mind primary evidence is and will always remain the best kind of evidence, still both types will be admitted when reliability is not in question. So that is the position we are taking. We consider primary evidence as more direct and more significant than secondary evidence, but we are not throwing secondary evidence overboard. We will consider and admit secondary evidence if there is no issue of -- serious issue of reliability. Now, I come straight away to one of the most fundamental principles that will guide the Trial Chamber, and that is the Trial Chamber will recognise and protect -- recognise and observe, keep in its mind at all times Article 21(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal which gives the accused presumption of innocence. This presumption - and I'm saying nothing which is new - this presumption of innocence places on the Prosecution the burden of establishing the guilt of the accused. Basically by this we mean that the Prosecution will have the burden of proving all the facts and circumstances which are material and necessary for -- to constitute the crimes charged and in addition also the accused's criminal responsibility. I wish to make it clear because sometimes this is misunderstood that the burden that I have mentioned remains on the Prosecution throughout the entire trial; it never changes. In accordance with Rule 87(A), the Prosecution must establish the accused's guilt beyond reasonable doubt, and at the end of the trial we will determine whether or not the ultimate result of the ensemble of all the evidence is weighty and convincing enough to establish beyond reasonable doubt the facts alleged and ultimately the guilt of the accused as charged in the indictment. The corollary of the principle that I have just touched upon is that the accused has a right to remain silent and this Trial Chamber will respect at all times that right. As a result we wish to make it clear that silence as such, silence as such, on the part of the accused may not and will not be used as evidence to prove his guilt and may and will not be interpreted at any time as an admission of guilt. In matters of admissibility of evidence, the Trial Chamber recognises that this is a unique Tribunal in which we've had the confluence of various systems, common law principles, continental law or civil law traditions, and there has been a very healthy melange of the procedural mixtures and each Judge that has come forward has brought with him the best parts of the system in which he or she have been brought up, and we have put these practices, these rules of procedure, to the best use possible in this Tribunal. As a result I'm making it also clear - and we've discussed this thoroughly amongst ourselves - that we do not feel ourselves bound or stuck to any particular system, be it the common law or the continental law, et cetera. We have our Rules of Evidence and Procedure, and those are the guiding -- the guidelines that we follow first and foremost. There's also the Statute which more or less also gives us an indication of what we need to follow. But what will be our beacon throughout the whole trial will be our determination to be inspired by the need for a fair determination of any matter that happens to be before us at any given time. So basically if we need to decide on any particular matter that arises, we will decide it not in terms of any particular system of law but according to the rule which we will agree at the time would amount to a fair determination of the matter. We also believe that in the context of our rules the approach of the Statute of the Tribunal -- of this Tribunal and also the approach of the various Trial Chambers that have been dealing with cases here has been to lay down a framework or a structure which is conceived in the broadest terms possible. And in particular, as you know, we started off under the umbrella of the Statute as almost a pure common-law Tribunal here, but we have incorporated a lot from other systems as we went along. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond The rules that we will be applying will always and at all times have due regard to the accused's right to a fair and public hearing. As such, we consider ourselves as having -- as carrying the burden, the responsibility, of ensuring that the trial is fair and as expeditious as possible and that the proceedings are at all times conducted in accordance with the rules with full respect to the procedural and substantive rights of your client, Madam Vidovic, but also because this is the responsibility of this Tribunal, but also for the protection of witnesses and victims. We will also keep in our mind the responsibility of this Tribunal to strive in favour and forward in the direction of trying to achieve and promote reconciliation in the territory of ex-Yugoslavia. The question of admissibility of evidence before this Tribunal is, as you know, governed by Section 3 of our rules. I refer you in particular to Rule 89(A) which makes it clear, in addition to what I have stated earlier, that the Trial Chamber shall not be bound by national rules of evidence, whether representing the common law or the civil law. The purpose of the rules is basically to promote a fair and expeditious trial, and the Trial Chamber reserves for itself as much flexibility as possible which it considers necessary in order to be able to achieve this goal. But there are a few items that arise from the common law system which I need to touch upon. In contrast to the common law where questions of admissibility and exclusion of evidence -- where questions of admissibility and exclusion of evidence occupy a very prominent place in criminal proceedings, the 13 provisions, section 3 of our rules, which regulate almost the totality of evidentiary matters and proceedings do not contain a detailed set of technical rules relating to this issue. As such, we interpret this as an indication that in establishing the set of rules in section 3, this Tribunal made sure that each Trial Chamber is not hindered in its search for the truth. Indeed, in our opinion, the most important rule in this context is Rule 89 itself, which lists the general evidentiary provisions. In subrule (B) of that Rule provides that: "In cases not otherwise provided for in this Section, the Chamber shall apply rules of evidence which shall best favour a determination of the matter before it and are consonant with the spirit of the Statute and the general principles of law." We also look at subrule (C) of Rule 89 as permitting the Chamber to admit any relevant evidence with probative value. Subrule 89(E) allows a Trial Chamber to request verification of the authenticity of evidence obtained out of court. It is clear that the approach adopted in the Rules is one that favours the admissibility of evidence provided it is -- provided it is relevant and has probative value. Irrelevant evidence must be and will be excluded in a most unequivocal way. And this we are determined upon because it is in the interest of a fair and expeditious trial. These considerations - which are not something which the Trial Chamber is stating for the first time, by no means - have resulted in a generally uniform tendency of the various Trial Chambers of this Tribunal towards admitting evidence in the first place, leaving its weight to be assessed when all the evidence is being considered by the Trial Chamber in the deliberation of its final decision. This will, therefore, in principle be the practice of this Trial Chamber. Another conspicuous practice that has been followed by the Trial Chambers of this Tribunal, and which will be followed also by this Trial Chamber, is that the general rules relating to the exclusion of evidence applied in common law systems, such as you Mr. Jones, and I used to, will not be followed as a rule. The main reason for this is very obvious -- or should be very obvious for you and also for anyone coming from such jurisdictions, these rules, in their essence, have been mostly developed within a context of a system of trial by jury, which is not the case here, as you know. In a trial-by-jury system, there is always the absolute and imperative need to keep away from the lay jurors prejudicial material of little or of no probative value which may be difficult to remove from their minds once they have heard it or seen it, as anyone who has presided over trials by jury, like I have, know very well. Therefore, please do remember at all times in your submissions on probative value and relevance, et cetera, that you are dealing with professional Judges with baggage of experience, considerable experience that we have each brought with us here and that we are not lay jurors. This Trial Chamber -- for this Trial Chamber this is very, very important. I come to the guidelines proper, and I will be dealing first with a set of guidelines that relate specifically to the admissibility of evidence. The first guideline that you should bear in mind in the course of this trial is that there is a basic distinction which is very clear to us between the legal admissibility of documentary evidence and the Trial Chamber's ultimate judgement as to its weight. The second guideline is that we are telling you that we will reject evidence if we are not satisfied of its relevance and probative value. Basically this brings me or leads me straight to the burden of proof with respect to relevance and probative value. The position we will be taking is that the burden of proof with respect to these two issues, relevance and probative value, lies with the party or on the party seeking to introduce a particular piece of evidence. However, we make a distinction between Prosecution and Defence. The Trial Chamber will follow the principle that the Prosecution must prove relevance, probative value, and reliability of evidence it seeks to bring into -- or evidence it seeks to bring forward beyond reasonable doubt if that issue comes up, whereas the Defence is only required to prove the admissibility of its evidence on the balance of probabilities. The third guideline is that the mere - and this we need to make very clear with you - the mere admission of a document into evidence does not in itself signify that the statements contained in that document will necessarily be deemed to be an accurate portrayal of the facts. Factors -- in addition, factors such as authenticity and proof of ownership will naturally assume great importance in the Trial Chamber's final assessment of the weight to be attached to each and every individual piece of evidence. We agree and we want you to know that the threshold standard for the admission of evidence in terms of introducing it into the proceedings should not and will not be set excessively high. And this is in line with the practice assumed by the majority of Trial Chambers in this Tribunal. We have chosen this approach - in other words, of not setting an excessively high threshold for the admission of evidence - because we consider that many a time documents are sought to be admitted in evidence not as the ultimate proof of guilt or innocence but to prove -- but to provide a context and perhaps a more complete picture presented by the evidence in general. The fourth guideline: The fact that we may at some point in the course of the proceedings rule for or against the admissibility of some particular document or other piece of evidence will not present us from reversing that ruling at a later stage, particularly if further evidence emerges which is relevant to the admissibility of that piece of evidence exposed. So this is a right which is, I consider, an inherent right which we will reserve for ourselves throughout the entire process. Next guideline. When objections are raised on grounds of authenticity -- and we are mentioning this now because this is one issue that we will be dealing with at the very early stages of this trial. So when objections are raised on grounds of authenticity, the Trial Chamber will follow the practice this Tribunal has previously adopted and my Trial Chamber has previously adopted in the other cases in which I have sat; namely, to admit documents, video recordings, and even telephone intercepts unless the admission of these pieces of appears to be manifestly inappropriate to do. And then everything goes in a big basket that we will have -- we will be carrying with us to the end of this trial when we will consider the whole of the evidence tendered and decide what Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond weight to give to the -- to each and every one of the documents tendered as well as to the ensemble of the evidence. There is no blanket prohibition and there will be no blanket prohibition on the admission of documents simply on the grounds that their purported order has not been called to testify. Similarly we also want to make it clear that an unsigned and unstemmed document does not a priori render it void of authenticity in the mind of this Trial Chamber. Factors such as proof of authorship will naturally assume great importance as we go along, and these are matters, together with authenticity, that we will determine in the final exercise of this Trial Chamber before rendering its final judgement. And I come now to hearsay evidence. Again, this is a major departure from what Mr. Jones and myself and you, Ms. Sellers, and others are used to. The practice of this Tribunal with regard to hearsay evidence is much more -- which is much broader than it is in common law jurisdictions. I prefer to address this matter by referring to what is now considered to be a classic pronouncement by this Trial Chamber -- by this Tribunal, and I'm referring to the dictum of the Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski appeal judgement. Basically it is well-settled in the practice and in the jurisprudence of this Tribunal that hearsay evidence is admissible. And after having been here for three years, I honestly believe that there is no way such trials could proceed and bear fruit either way for or against the Prosecution or for or against the accused, unless we admit hearsay evidence. Basically this means that relevant out-of-court statements which we consider probative will be admitted because they are admissible under Rule 89(C). I refer you to what was stated in Aleksovski, but I see that we have quite an audience in the gallery and perhaps it might be worth repeating the words of the Appeals Chamber. The Appeals Chamber stated in Aleksovski that: "The Trial Chambers have a broad discretion under Rule 89(C) to admit relevant hearsay evidence. Since such evidence is admitted to prove the truth of its contents, the Trial Chamber must be satisfied that it is reliable for that purpose, in the sense of being voluntary, fruitful, and trustworthy and also appropriate. For this purpose the Trial Chamber may consider both the content of the hearsay statement and the circumstances under which the evidence arose." Or as Judge Stephen described it: "The probative value of a hearsay statement will depend upon the context and the character of the evidence in question. The absence of the opportunity to cross-examine the person who made the statements and whether the hearsay is firsthand or more removed or more remote are also relevant to the probative value of the evidence. The fact that the evidence is hearsay does not necessarily deprive it of probative value. But it is acknowledged" - and this is very important to remember, both of you - "that the weight or value to be afforded to that evidence will usually be less than that given to the testimony of a witness who has given it under a form of oath" - and in our system, under solemn declaration - "and who has been cross-examined, although even this will depend upon the infinitely variable circumstances which surround hearsay evidence." I come now to what in common law jurisdictions is referred to as the best rule, which today is a far cry from what it used to be in years past. In determining the matters before this Trial Chamber and issues before this Trial Chamber, the so-called best evidence rule will be applied provided that such evidence is evidently available. And you all know that we are dealing with cases where it is very difficult sometimes to obtain what would be considered as the best evidence. This essentially means that the Trial Chamber will, where possible, rely on the best evidence available in the circumstances of the case, and the parties are directed to regulate the production of their evidence along these lines when possible. What is the best evidence will of course depend on the particular circumstances attached to each document and the complexity of this case and the investigations that preceded it as well as the difficulties that this Tribunal sometimes encounters in its efforts to acquire documents and other pieces of evidence. The Trial Chamber is also aware that this rule has lost much of its importance in some common law jurisdictions and we will consequently, in applying the residues of this best evidence rule, exercise our discretion in the spirit that lies at the basis of this Statute and our Rules. I have a final word on circumstantial evidence. This will -- we will obviously return to in the final judgement, but we were torn between the idea of whether we should mention it now or whether we should just leave it and then tell you later how we considered circumstantial evidence. We decided to include it now as part of the guidelines, although strictly speaking it is not a guideline in itself. But it is an information that we are giving you so that you would be able to know what importance to attach to circumstantial evidence which, as in all other trials that I am aware of, will be important in this case as well. We consider circumstantial evidence as being that evidence of circumstances surrounding an event or an offence from which a fact at issue may be reasonably inferred. We realise that many a time crimes are committed when witnesses are not present and since in criminal trials, especially in cases like the ones before this Tribunal, the possibility of establishing the matter charged by direct and positive testimony of eyewitnesss or by conclusive documents is more often than not problematic or outright unavailable. Circumstantial evidence may become a critical ingredient in a trial, and this I say both in respect to your case and in respect to your case. Circumstantial evidence, as we may well experience in this case, may assume great importance. The individual items of such evidence may by themselves be insufficient to establish a fact, but taken together their collective and cumulative effect may be very revealing and sometimes decisive. And we are telling you this in order to prepare you, because at the end of the trial when we embark on our deliberations, on our final exercise, we are going to put together the circumstantial evidence that would have been brought forward -- put to us in the course of the trial, and these are the principles that we will be adopting. We believe also that it is no derogation of evidence to say that this or that piece of evidence is circumstantial. So do bear this in mind, please. Therefore, we will not consider circumstantial evidence to be of less substance than direct evidence, and that is a matter -- as a matter of principle. We wish also to draw your attention to Rule 95 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence which provides that evidence which is obtained by methods which cast substantial doubt on reliability or evidence that is antithetical to or would seriously damage the proceedings is not admissible, and we will take a very firm stand if anything of this sort emerges in the course of the trial. The Trial Chamber makes it clear at the very outset that statements which are not voluntary but are obtained from suspects by -- or even by prospective witnesses by oppressive conduct cannot pass the test under Rule 95 and will not be admitted. Naturally the burden of proving that a statement was voluntary lies on the party seeking to introduce it, whereby the standards discussed already earlier on which I referred you to will be applicable. If one reads the various rules or some of the rules under Section 3 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, one gets the impression that the rules implicitly require that reliability be a component of admissibility, and indeed following previous case law of this Tribunal on this matter, we want you to know that we agree completely that reliability is indeed an inherent and implicit component of each element of admissibility. This is particularly so within the context of hearsay evidence that I mentioned to you earlier. Because if hearsay evidence which is offered is unreliable, then it can neither be relevant nor have probative value; therefore, such evidence, if we come across it, will be inadmissibility in terms of subrule 89(C). However, this is restricted only to hearsay evidence; I'm making it clear. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond With regard to other documentary evidence, we wish to make it clear that the determination of the issue of reliability when it arises should not be and will not be seen as a separate first step in assessing a piece of evidence of it for admission. In other words, we will make a distinction in the importance as a prerequisite that we attach to the element of reliability. Whether we are dealing -- depending on whether we are dealing with hearsay evidence or other types of evidence. With regard to other types of evidence, particularly documentary evidence which is not tendered as hearsay, reliability will not be considered as a first step in assessing whether that document should be admitted or not. Therefore the notion of establishing indicia of reliability ought not to be confused with having admissibility predicated on proof of reliability. If we were to adopt a different system, we would be making room or leaving room for you to evade the well-established case law of this Tribunal. We wish to remind you that we consider ourselves to be the guardians of the procedural and substantive rights of the accused. The accused can remain assured that we will protect these procedural and substantive rights at all costs throughout the entire trial. A trial, as you know, is more often than not a very complex journey in search of the truth. And as such, we considered that questions of admissibility of evidence do not arise only when one of the parties raises an objection to a particular piece of evidence sought to be brought forward by the other party. There may be other instances where we would feel the need to intervene ourselves. Naturally -- I mean I want to make it clearly also that when there is no objection to the authenticity of a document, the task of admitting that particular document will be made much easier. However, this Trial Chamber has an inherent right and duty to ensure that only evidence that qualifies, which qualifies for admission under the rules, will be admitted. Therefore, it may turn out to be necessary from time to time - and this did happen in other cases in which I was involved - the Trial Chamber will, if necessary, intervene ex officio to exclude from these proceedings those pieces of evidence which in our opinion, for one or more of the reasons laid out in the rules, ought not to be admitted in evidence. I hope we have made ourselves clear on these issues. Having touched on matters of admissibility, I come to the end. These may sound to you as matters that need not be raised, but in every trial there are incidents. I have learned during my stay here that not only Judges come from different systems, but also members of the staff, legal officers, registrars, and counsel come from different. And there are some matters that we feel very strongly upon, particularly as regards contacts with the Trial Chamber and with our staffs -- members of our staffs as well as the relations that we expect amongst yourselves throughout the entire conduct. So forgive me if I am going to repeat what you already know and what you already believe in, but they will be put on record, this is what we expect. We work in a system where, as you know, ex parte meetings between the Trial Chamber - and, could be the Prosecution, could be the Defence, you have the right to ask for ex parte meetings as well - are possible. Now, these are possible because they have been introduced in the procedure of this Tribunal and recognised as such. When a -- one of the parties seeks an ex parte meeting with the Trial Chamber, the other party will be informed. There is no way that we will hold an ex parte meeting with you, for example, without informing the Prosecution that we are having an ex parte meeting with you; and there is no way we will hold an ex parte meeting with the Prosecution without informing that we have an ex parte meeting with the Prosecution. There is also the practice that if, say, the Prosecution have filed an ex parte motion, they will also inform you that they have filed an ex parte motion. We require this as a practice to be adopted without exception. It does not mean that you need to tell the other party what the contents of the motion are, because most of the time these matters relate to the personal safety and security of some individuals and need to be treated with the utmost confidentiality. But, in other words, in meeting with requests from either of you for ex parte meetings, we might want to assure you that this will be done in the most transparent manner. That's rule number one. We require from each one of you, all members of the Prosecution team, all members of the Defence team, to demonstrate the utmost respect, integrity, and courtesy to all the officers of this Trial Chamber and of the Tribunal and the staff members of the Trial Chamber. And not only that, we have here with us interpreters, technicians. These individuals work hard. They have a very difficult job, particularly the interpreters. We request of you hat at all times we respect them as individuals and also the hard work and the long hours in which they are required to work. There will be hitches, there will be problems, there will be problems also with interpretation, but the approach is the most important part of it. The interpreters have a difficult task; they are here to help us. Sometimes mistakes happen. We have to be patient, we have to be tolerant. Many a time we will be calling on them to stay with us a few extra minutes, and infallibly we have found the cooperation of both the interpreters and the technicians. So, please, respect and courtesy ought to be the rules of the road. The parties are reminded that you should not try to influence in any way or communicate with any one of us, any of the three Judges, with any of our officers, and with any of our staff - legal staff in particular - by means which are prohibited by Statute or by the rules, or by the rules -- respective rules of professional conduct. You have your own. The Office of the Prosecution have got their own set of rules of conduct. So I need not preach on what these -- the applicable rules are, I'm just reminding you and I will not say anything further. Naturally there will be the need to communicate on several matters, like administrative matters, like housekeeping matters, like giving prior notice that a motion is to be expected, or handing a complementary advance copy of a motion. There are many instances where there must be some kind of communication, liaison, between our staff and either the Prosecution or the Defence. The rule of the road is no abuse of any of the channels of communication that become necessary as we go along. The legal staff, our legal staff, are fully aware of these rules. I don't need to preach to them either because they have these rules set out since a long time ago. In your relations we expect each party to recognise the representatives of the other party as professional colleagues first and foremost and not only as adversaries. And we expect you to act fairly, honestly and courteously towards one other; that's important. And we will intervene if at any time this comes short of our expectations. It does happen. There will be moments of tension, there will be moments of attrition sometimes. But, please, always try to keep calm, moderate your words, and maintain fairness, honesty, and courtesy towards one another. Last but not least, I left it to the very end, not because it is not important but because we attach a lot of importance to it. We request of you that you do not resort to any means that have no other substantial purpose than to embarrass, delay, or burden the Victims and Witnesses Unit. We will not allow you to use coercive or other methods of obtaining evidence in the course of testimonies here, other coercive or in any other manner which is not acceptable to us. Many a time we will be dealing with persons that have past experienced severe trauma in their lives, traumas that none of us have had to face in our respective lives, and in addition giving evidence on those events is an added trauma. So you have every right to put questions, both Prosecution and Defence, but you also have a corresponding duty to be courteous to these witnesses, especially if they happen to be witnesses, victims. So that brings me to an end of the guidelines. If -- before proceeding to other matters, if there are matters, issues, that you would like to raise arising out of these guidelines which will be handed down to Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond you in writing, as I said, early next week, polished a little bit and handed down formally to you. But if there are any matters that you would like to raise now or remarks you would like to raise now, make now, please feel free to do so, in which case we will proceed to the rest of the agenda of today. I see none. So we will proceed to what I described yesterday as -- in very broad terms as housekeeping matters which are necessary to deal with and dispose of before we start with the first witness. Ideally, as I explained to you both during the pre-trial conference and yesterday, some of the issues that we have outstanding should have on paper been dealt with at the pre-trial stage, but they couldn't. And in addition, several other issues arose both within the same time -- at the same time frame of the pre-trial conference and subsequently with the result that we find ourselves starting this trial with a significant number of pending motions. I will be appealing to the cooperation of both the Prosecution and the Defence today to make it possible for us to determine or to decide some of these motions orally today, and if the motions are such that would call for follow-up by means of a written decision, we will do so, otherwise we will remain with the oral decision. For example, I learned yesterday that with regard to the motion for protective measures, there's only one witness that you have objections, the rest you don't. So I take it that we should be in a position to decide at least with respect to those other witnesses where there is no objection. And this is how I intend to proceed along this morning. Let's start with the first outstanding motion. And members of the public will notice when I mention the dates why these motions are still pending. The first motion is a confidential Prosecution motion for leave to amend the Prosecution list of witnesses. This was filed on the 28th of September. You know that while this case was still before Trial Chamber III, there was a motion by the Prosecution to have some witnesses added to the list; that was granted by the previous Trial Chamber. Then subsequently the Prosecution came up with -- is there a problem, Madam Vidovic? Okay. Then the Prosecution came up with a fresh motion to which the Defence responded on the 1st of October. As discussed yesterday, the witness statements have now finally been disclosed to the Defence. So I presume at least, if I read your objection properly, Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic, that this being so, now that the witness statements have been disclosed to you. We do not really have any substantive objection on your part which would make it impossible for us to proceed along the lines of the motion of the Prosecution. If you confirm this to me, then we can actually grant the motion of the Prosecution this morning orally. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour, except that we expect yet another thing. We would like to receive copies of their statements in a language that the accused understands, but that is no hindrance in terms of continuing the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So now let's make sure that we have covered everything. The motion includes or the list includes also the first of the Prosecution witness Racine Manas. We have received the statement, together with the accompanying documents. I want to make sure that you have as well? Okay. And also of those five witnesses, I'm not going to mention the names because I'm not quite sure if any of them enjoy protective measures, but I want to make sure that the five witnesses to which you made specific reference in your response you also have received their statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have received the statements of those witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the motion also covered witnesses Kelly and Tedder, and I think yesterday you made it clear that you are happy with the application of Rule 89(F) and that you do not require these persons for cross-examination. So let's make the first step forward. Mr. Registrar, the Trial Chamber, having seen the confidential Prosecution motion for leave to amend the Prosecution list of witnesses filed on the 28th of September, 2004, as well as the confidential response filed by the Defence on the 1st of October, 2004, and after having heard the parties, grants the motion of the Prosecution as requested. I don't think that this needs to be followed by a written version of the decision. There is a matter that as it is now I am going to raise because I want to make it clear. Yesterday the Prosecution filed a motion to admit the written statements of witnesses Mr. Barney Kelly and Stephen Tedder pursuant to 89(F), these two persons I just referred to a couple of minutes ago. I want to make sure, first of all, that you have receive -- you have been served with this motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have been served. Thank you. I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, you have already confirmed also that you do not object to these statements and that you do not want to cross-examine the witnesses. Now, apropos -- yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. What you said is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to clear up a matter which is strictly legal and which I think we can surmount. There was a decision, an interlocutory decision by the Appeals Chamber in the Milosevic case referring to Rule 89(F) which is being invoked in this motion by the Prosecution and to which you agree, and basically the test that the Appeals Chamber have set down or laid down for applying -- being able to apply this rule is the following: Number one, the witness must be present in a courtroom or in court. So basically one of the most essential requirements according to the Appeals Chamber is the presence of a witness here, which is obviously what the Prosecution has been trying to avoid. I mean, the whole idea is not to have these witnesses brought forward either from Australia or Canada where they reside, otherwise it just wouldn't make sense in applying for or asking for the application of Rule 89(F), et cetera. The position as I see it is this: That if the Defence had not objected to the application of Rule 89(F) but insisted on the right to cross-examine the witness, then obviously the presence of the witness would have been required in any case and this would not have constituted a problem. But if the Defence is waiving their rights to cross-examine these two witnesses, I honestly don't see the practicality of having these two persons brought over. As I said, one is Australian and one is Canadian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. Patricia Sellers will address this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I could, good morning. The situation of the two witnesses in terms of where they are is slightly different. It is correct that Mr. Tedder is in Australia. Mr. Kelly is here in the building. He is currently working as an investigator. When the offer was made to the Defence where they accept the declarations, we were already in the process of having Mr. Tedder come from Australia because there was a possibility that they would not accept that, and certainly we had informed the investigator, Mr. Kelly, that there was a chance that he might be called and might be asked to testify before the Tribunal. When the Defence decided that they would accept the statements and the attendant documents attached to the statements, it appears that they did not want to cross-examine either Mr. Tedder or Mr. Kelly, and therefore the 89(F) motion was put in as it is. But certainly they had the ability -- and the Prosecution was more than willing to make the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond witnesses appear physically. For one witness it's just a matter of coming down a couple of floors within this very building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. But that solves it with one of the two persons but not with regard to the other. But let me finish this so that you can address actually the other requirements as established by the Appeals Chamber. Rule number one is the witness must be present in court. Rule number two is the witness must be available for cross-examination and questioning by the Judges. Right? And this now doesn't depend any longer on the Defence, and it is very difficult for us to take the position of saying we accept the contents of these statements and we do not want to cross-examine the contents of the witnesses. And last but not least, the witness must be in a position to attest that the statement accurately reflects his or her declaration. Now, again how are we going to surmount this? It could be surmounted by an additional declaration, a declaration that they certify as correct the statements that you will be filing in court. But again, I mean, what lies beyond -- behind this third requirement is that if the person is not present here in court, he is not physically present to see what statement is actually being provided to the Trial Chamber. So when you look at these three rules, you see -- you suddenly see the logic behind them requiring the presence in the court, in the Tribunal, of these two persons. If there is agreement amongst you that none of these two persons are required physically here, then I think we will be able to take that into consideration in our decision whether to admit the statements of these two persons under Rule 89(F) or not. Definitely, definitely, we cannot renounce to our right to sort of examine or -- not exactly cross-examine but examine these two witnesses if necessary. So one solution could be admitting the statements under Rule 89(F), if there is no objection on the part of the Defence, with the caveat that at any time we may require these two persons to come over and give evidence on the contents or on the authenticity -- don't misunderstand me. I don't want to throw any doubts on the authenticity of the statements. But as I said we are the guardians of the rights of the accused. So please tell us whether you are -- whether you could live with such an arrangement, in which case we will deliberate later on and come back to you after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Your Honour, the Prosecution certainly will place themselves in our hands, and we understand the position that you're in and the discretion that you have to use in terms of your own objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I thank you, Madam Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The position of the Defence was really designed to assist the Court in saving time and wasting resources by not bringing witnesses here when there's nothing contentious whatsoever in their statements as far as we are concerned. So we wrote to the Prosecution and we suggested, just purely on the text of 89(F) as it appears in the Rules, that that appeared to be an enabling provision which would enable Your Honours to admit a written statement. We're aware, of course, of the jurisprudence in the Milosevic, although that might be the decision where there was fairly strong dissent from Judge Hunt, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Hunt was dissenting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed. But we were basing ourselves on that text and certainly the approach which Your Honour suggests seems eminently sensible, and we're happy with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The problem why we definitely cannot waive our right to bring these two persons over and have them examined by us is that we only got their statement yesterday, I think. So at the end of the day, none of us has read these statements, and if we really want to respect and protect the rights of the accused, we have to reserve our right, after having read them, to see whether it's the case of bringing these two persons over to us to answer questions. But we certainly do not -- are not prepared to waive what is reserved to us not as a right but as a duty. Okay? So we will come unless there is an agreement already --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are in agreement, so we can actually decide this here and now. So the Trial Chamber is seized of the motion filed by the Prosecution on the 6th of October, 2004, to admit the written statements of witnesses Barney Kelly and Stephen Tedder pursuant to 89(F). The Trial Chamber has heard the submissions of the Defence in regard to this motion. The Defence are not objecting to the admission of these -- or the written statements of these two witnesses pursuant to the said Rule, and they also declared that they are waiving their right to cross-examine the two witnesses. The Trial Chamber makes reference to the decision by the Appeals Chamber in the interlocutory decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Milosevic case in relation to the test that is applicable for Rule 89(F), which, inter alia, requires the presence of the accused [sic] and in order to be in a position -- to be available for cross-examination and questioning by the Judges. In addition, also the presence of the accused may be required to attest the statement, that the statement accurately reflects his or her declaration. Because of this final -- two final requirements for the application of Rule 89(F), the Trial Chamber, taking into consideration in particular the non-objection on the part of the Defence, admits -- grants the motion, admits the written statements of witnesses Barney Kelly and Stephen Tedder pursuant to Rule 89(F), reserving for itself, however, the right to ask the Prosecution to bring forward either or both of the two witnesses for examination by the Trial Chamber or for attestation that their statement accurately reflects their respective declaration, should the need arise. So that disposes of the second motion. And I must acknowledge the cooperation of both the Prosecution and the Defence. This all goes well for the rest of this trial. We come to the first real problem which I touched upon yesterday. We need to decide today how we are going to proceed on this matter. I'm referring to the Prosecution confidential motion filed on the 27th of September for admission of written statements of witnesses pursuant to Rule 92 bis (C). We are dealing with two categories of persons, two categories of witnesses. Witnesses who allegedly are unable to come to give evidence because of serious -- ill health or serious health problems; and the second category, witnesses who are longer with the living. The Defence, as I explained yesterday, filed a confidential response to the Prosecution motion on the 30th of September objecting to the admission of all statements, also making submissions. Yesterday I touched upon this motion and also the response, particularly since upon receiving from the Prosecution the list of the first batch of witnesses they intend to bring forward, I noticed that two of these witnesses were amongst the three that are mentioned in this motion of the 27th of September; in other words, they are witnesses that the Prosecution has not yet been authorised to bring forward under the regime of Rule 92 bis (C). We also yesterday explained that we attached to this matter importance because there are legal issues involved, particularly in relation to the witness who is dead, and that there is absolutely no way this witness can be cross-examined by the Defence. And also I'm realising that the decision that we will ultimately have to reach on the other two witnesses very much depends on the verification of what you allege as the basis for your request and also the consequences of these witnesses not coming over and therefore not being made available for cross-examination. These are serious matters. This is not a case where we have hundreds and hundreds of witnesses and where one could make allowances here because one thing could make up for another. So we expressed our availability for debate on this issue should the need arise. Only that Mr. Wubben stood up yesterday and informed us that his team had been working around the clock day and night on elaborating written submissions on the matter which was welcomed news, because it will highlight I'm sure the various salient features of the issues involved and which would enable you to respond either in writing or after having taking stock of the written submissions and after having been given sufficient time, we can then have the matter debated here. We would dedicate as much time as is necessary but not more than one session to debate it. And then this is definitely something that we will need to decide in writing. Some of the matters have been dealt with by other Trial Chambers before. I would say some others haven't been dealt with or need to be dealt with more thoroughly in this trial. So that is the -- yes, Madam Vidovic. I haven't seen the submissions as of yet. Have you filed them, Mr. Wubben? Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the submissions were filed and Your Honours and both learned counsel were offered courtesy copies yesterday so that you would be able to review them prior to today's session. We understand your time constraints. But the official registry copies might only have been available today. We wanted to have the Chamber's copies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They were only given to us this morning. This morning, this is what we received this morning. Okay. So I take it that you have filed it. I still don't see it here -- no, okay. All right. I have it here. What is the -- what is your preference, Madam Vidovic, if you are in a position give us a preference, to state a preference?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have received the response of the Prosecution to our response, and I believe that it is in the interest of the proceedings to respond straight away, that is to say, in order to apply Rule 90 bis (C). We have carried out investigations and I think it is very important for the Chamber and for the Prosecution to hear of the results. As for these three witnesses, there are two categories involved, as you've already said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. But in -- just in case you will be dealing with medical records or -- et cetera in relation to either of two of them, please tell me beforehand so that we will go into private session because these are matters that need -- shouldn't be made public. So please do guide me as you go along. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then I shall first speak about the second category of witnesses, namely Bogicevic, Veseljko, and Witness Novka Bozic. As for Witness Veseljko Bogicevic, we highlighted in our motion that we have reasons to believe that he did not die and this is why. The Prosecution asked for Witness Novka Bozic to be under Rule 92 bis (C). We checked this information and we learned that this person was not dead and finally the Prosecution confirmed this. This was something that caution does that we should be very careful and that we have to look at all the materials related to these witnesses. Had we not done this, there would have been abuse of Rule 92 bis (C). Therefore, we checked all the documents very carefully, all the documents supporting Witness Veseljko Bogicevic. Your Honours, please look at annex 3 of the Prosecution motion dated the 27th of September, 2004, this is a statement given to the Prosecution, and please compare it to annex 4, namely the death certificate related to Mr. Veseljko Bogicevic. You will notice straight away that the dates of birth differ in these two documents. This immediately led us to a further investigation. We checked this out unofficially. We checked the personal code number of citizens. We looked at the code number that is in the death certificate -- actually, I wish to draw your attention to the following: That in our system - and that is probably the way it is everywhere in the world - every person has a code number of their own. We immediately noticed that this personal code number, personal identification number, has a certain logic of its own, according to our system, could not be the identification number of Veseljko Bogicevic. We checked this out and established that Veseljko Bogicevic was not registered under this number and that this number actually belongs to a person called Begic [phoen]. Then we tried to approach the matter in a more direct fashion. I am sorry that I do not have an English translation of this document here. We worked on all of this late last night. You realise that we received the motion only yesterday. And we established that the person that gave a statement to the Prosecution, that is to say Bogicevic Veseljko, was born in Ratkovici, municipality of Srebrenica, and this person's number is 0404940183123. So this document that was provided to us by the Prosecution for Bogicevic, Veseljko, born on the 7th of August [as interpreted], 2002 does not pertain to Bogicevic, Veseljko, for whom the Prosecutor wishes to apply Rule 92 bis (C). I shall tell you that I received this information by making checks at the federal institute of statistics, which is relevant for all this citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I believe that the same kind of check could have been carried out by the Prosecutors, too. Therefore we express our sincere doubt in terms of the authenticity of these documents. I kindly ask the Judges to bear this in mind, and in terms of further proceedings I must say that yesterday the Prosecutor said that Oric was trying to build a smokescreen around the documents and the authenticity of the documents. Allow me to say today that somebody else is making this smokescreen or this camouflage net around the documents, and we are trying to penetrate through it. I wish to draw the attention of our colleagues, the Prosecutors, to that because of all the things you told us today in terms of fair play between the parties in the proceedings. When objecting to the authenticity of the documents pertaining to Mrs. -- Novka Bozic, we never said or wrote that the Prosecution perhaps intentionally obtained false death certificates, and this Defence would never say any such thing. On the contrary, we said something completely different, that these certificates were falsified, forged, and that it was our duty to draw your attention to that. This is not to say that we are blaming the Prosecution for that, but we certainly believe that the Prosecution is duty-bound to pay due attention to such matters and to assess the evidence before them. Believe me, we are going to deal with each and every document that gets into our hands in the same way, although our resources are limited. We are not going to sleep, as we didn't sleep last night, but we are going to come to the facts. In paragraph 10 of their response -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you're coming to a fresh point, I think we need to have a break now because we've just passed our time by a few minutes. We'll have a 25-minute break and we'll resume at 11.00. We'll resume at 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, permit me before I continue for the sake of the accuracy of the transcript I do apologise, the date of death was not the 7th of April but from the document that was delivered to us I mistakenly said the 7th of August. I apologise. The reason for the error is that I did not get enough sleep last night, as I said. I shall continue very briefly and then I will ask for us to go into private session. In paragraph 10 of the response by the Prosecution of the 6th of October, 2004, it says that the Defence erroneously suggested that the Prosecutor intentionally changed Bogicevic's statement in order to create a false impression. I wish to draw your attention to footnote number 3 of our reply of the 30th of September, 2004, on page 3, paragraph 9. We said the Defence does not suspect the Prosecutor of intentionally changing the statement in order to create a false impression and so on and so forth. We could not have been clearer, and I beg to have our submissions interpreted in future in the spirit in which they were written, because we are doing our utmost to respect the rules of this Tribunal. Your Honours, I hope that we are now in private session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not yet, Madam Vidovic. Registrar, could we go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we are back in open session. The reason why we were in private session is we were dealing with the medical condition of one of the persons mentioned in this motion and that we considered not to have debated in public. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's start with Novka Bozic. We are happy to learn, therefore, that this woman is alive and not dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution admits that it erred and is happy, and I think the Defence will join us in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also take it you that intend to bring her forward as a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, we do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that solves one-third of the problem. The other person who you say is dead Defence say is still alive. He was not a nobody. I mean, he was someone, at least from what I read, he was a public figure for some time. So I take it that it should not be that difficult to establish whether he is alive or he is dead. I don't know at this point in time. I am baffled, seriously baffled. At the same time, the points raised by the Defence, by Madam Vidovic, in relation to the death certificate that you exhibited, that you filed, do raise some question. I mean, after all we had also a certificate purporting to show that Madam Bozic was dead only to find out that we were talking of a different person and she is still alive. And kicking, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, she is. I would like to address the issues raised by Madam Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's tackle this first.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Novka Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, in particular those issues, Your Honour. Madam Vidovic pointed out within the death certificate several things. The Prosecutor would first like to demonstrate to Your Honours that let's look at the commmonalities of the death certificate and our information that the person is deceased. The death certificate shows the same name of the person. What Your Honours does not have before you is the statement of the deceased person. The Defence certainly does have this statement before them. If they look at it, they will also note that it is not only the same name of the person, the person's father has the same name, the person's wife has the same name, the person was born in the same place. The only difference that one could discern is that there is a slight difference in terms of the date of birth. The date of birth differs by three days. The Prosecution is uncertain as to whether that difference of three days - the 7th of April or the 3rd of April - is a typographical error on our part or the other. Thank you very much. In addition to that, I would like to inform Your Honours and certainly learned counsel that we are currently calling the family now, just to reassure Your Honours of the state of health or death of that person. We agree that it is a public figure and we certainly would like to convey that we would like to know not only the real and vital information, because to go to 92 bis (C) in many ways means that we reduce the evidence that we are allowed to present. We certainly do not intend to abuse 92 bis (C) as Defence counsel might have suggested, and we certainly do not intend to reduce the Prosecution's ability to present evidence. So If I could get back to Your Honours with this, our final bit of information, hopefully by the end of the session or as soon as possible. So in those manners I think we have met 92 bis (C)'s requirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In pursuing this matter could you also address, not now, obviously, with the relatives of the person you allege to be deceased, could you also pursue the question of the identification, personal identification number.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: We certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, that is one other area which has been touched upon by the Defence as a basis for their contention that this person is still alive or that the death certificate refers to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we certainly will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also have tried -- because we also do have his statement and unfortunately that's how I know that he was a prominent public figure. Unfortunately -- if you see there is -- the place of birth is the same, Ratkovici, Srebrenica. The place of death is supposedly Abdulici. Date of death is 7th August, 2002. It doesn't show father's name or anything else which could have helped us identify this person more. There is an indication of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if you would look on the first page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: ... but you don't find it on the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Sorry. On the first page of our statement - and I don't know what Your Honours are looking at, we have a cover page - and there it's clearly indicated the father's first name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you don't find it in the death certificate. This is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would draw your attention to the second page of the death certificate, on the second page of the death certificate, the translation is provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: And also the name of his wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Father Jovanka Bogicevic. Anyway, we need to establish whether this person is alive or dead. The death certificate shows that he was born on the 7th of April, 1940, and not on the 4th of April. So it could either be a mistake in the first page of your statement or a mistake in the death certificate; I don't know. But what could be the determining factor is the identity -- identification number. So maybe if you could check that with the members of his family, we could close the matter there. And that would leave us then with the question -- the legal submissions only as to whether this statement of a dead person who is not available for cross-examination should be admitted. And that will of course involve a full-scale discussion. So that is going to be attended to by you. The other person, Miladin Bogdanovic. I honestly feel confused. I have seen the date of the statement that you filed together with your motion, which goes back to 2000. I have seen the statement of the investigator which goes to October 2003. It says: "I interviewed the witness for the Prosecution in the case against Naser Oric named Bogdanovic Miladin on the 22nd day of October, 2003." And then there is a medical certificate - I don't need to go into details and therefore we can stay in open session - which seems to be dated at least on the 23rd of September, 2003, which deals with one aspect of his disease. At the same time -- let me find the response because what the Defence states is -- needs to be addressed anyway. I mean, it's -- basically referring to the medical reports that you attached to the motion. The Defence submits that the medical reports in themselves do not touch on the ability of the witness to speak or to carry on conversation. And in particular the second report, which is dated the 23rd of September, and I'm mentioning the date because it is very near to the date when your investigator went to interview him. The second report says that this person is conscious, orientated, able to communicate, somewhat hard-of-hearing, and walking with the help of a stick. Again, there is no mention in the report that this person is unable to speak. I don't think -- again, this is something that we will need to discuss between Judge Brydensholt, Eser, and myself. I don't think this puts us in a very happy situation because more or less within this same time frame - we're talking of September/October 2003 - while one certificate would not justify your request --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I address the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The statement of your investigator does justify it. So I think we will need to establish the medical condition of this person in some other manner, because I don't think that what we have is enough to enable us to reach a recent decision. I mean, we have got conflicting scenarios here as I see it. So you could, if you want, agree on a medical person who would visit this individual and report back to the -- to either one of you. I mean, you could agree on a person. That is something that you could do without the intervention, direct intervention of the Trial Chamber. If not, we will have to nominate -- appoint someone. At this point in time, I don't think it should be left to either of you. If it needs to be established, it will need to be established by an independent observer. Unless you agree on a person amongst yourselves, say a doctor in the area which you both have trust in. I mean, it could be done with the least expense possible, would not be nominated by the Tribunal. You could even share the expense among yourselves, and we will take account of his certificate in lieu of us having to nominate an independent individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be acceptable --

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will approach the Defence counsel -- excuse me, learned counsel. We will approach the Defence counsel with your suggestion. The Prosecution would just like to say that also you have available to you, if you did want to speak to our investigator, who it is significant saw him in a short time period afterwards but actually tried to speak to him and elicit conversation. But we will certainly approach counsel and determine the state of health and in particular the ability of this witness to communicate within the precepts of 92 bis (C), whether he is mentally or physically unable to testify orally at the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers, I do not doubt for a moment the evaluation made by your investigator, but again an investigator remains an investigator. And even if he came forward and testified on this and gave us his own personal evaluation, it's not going to solve the problem. Between October/September 2003 and now, another year has passed under the bridges. And the situation may have improved or may have worsened. As you know, people having the condition that this person has, the situation varies from time to time. So I think it needs to be established for the benefit of everyone and also to have something credible on which we can work and then reach a decision. It needs to be assessed by someone who is an expert -- a doctor, a medical doctor, in other words. I think what I suggested makes sense if it's workable, but you have to agree on a doctor. If not, we will appoint someone, someone -- we'll ask the registrar to inform us on who could be available to be appointed and then we will ask the registrar, direct the registrar to appoint him and examine this prospective witness. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. That's certainly acceptable to us to have an independent expert, and clearly an investigator of the Prosecution who isn't a neurosurgeon, isn't a doctor. It's not his job to evaluate that. And we'll discuss that with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: One thing I would say just now is we would like to request the Prosecution -- it may not arise now but in future to provide full translations as well as -- of these documents because in our response if it was one word which was important it was ability to communicate, and that was omitted from the summary translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you, Mr. Jones. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can discuss the arrangements with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I am going to close the debate on this motion now, here, the position being as follows: The Prosecution will report back to the Trial Chamber on its further investigations into the death or otherwise of Witness Veseljko Bogicevic. We don't need to address Novka Bozic because I take it that she is going to be brought forward as a witness. And you are going to find out -- discuss first whether you can agree on a doctor who will visit and examine this witness and then report back to us. In case of no agreement, then we will -- before we proceed with any further discussion on this motion, we will ask the registrar to appoint a doctor to do exactly the same and report -- issue a medical certificate to the Trial Chamber. Okay. We'll move to the next motion. On the 24th of September, 2004, the Prosecution filed another confidential motion for leave to add exhibits to its exhibit list -- to its exhibit list. The exhibit list that had been filed earlier in terms of Rule 65 ter. On the 27th of September, the Defence filed the confidential response to the Prosecution motion and -- objecting to the addition of five of the proposed additional exhibits. We discussed this matter very briefly during the pre-trial conference, as you remember. We gave the Prosecution the opportunity to file a reply, which they did on the 5th of October. In reality, having checked the date again, I have to say that it was filed late in terms of Rule 126 bis. Still, I will turn to the Defence, first to confirm that you have received it, and secondly to know whether you object for the introduction of this reply in the records of the case because it was filed late or whether you want to close a blind eye and keep the filing in the records as if it had been filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is always possible for the Trial Chamber to address the Defence and say you have filed it late. Could you make submissions on the issue. So I'm making the suggestion that you be practical. It's not something which is do or die for the Defence or for the outcome of the trial obviously. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, precisely. It may happen to us at some point as well, so we do not mind having things remain that way. I am going to respond very briefly. For example, when the exhumations expert is concerned, Mr. Stankovic, or whichever witness, we object to introducing this kind of voluminous evidence for a simple reason. It is video footage that is being tendered about exhumations, even those that were carried out outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, for example in Croatia, in Vukovar. If the Prosecutor is trying to prove that Stankovic in his career was engaged in exhumations, that is not being challenged. We are not going to object to that. Therefore, it is not necessary to add this kind of evidence. However, if we were to accept this kind of practice, that may mean that some day the Prosecution will try to show Mr. Gow lecturing to students or show his books so that we would know that he is a teacher. Therefore, it is not necessary to tender irrelevant evidence. As for the rest, as regards our other responses, we abide by what we originally said in our first response and objection to the Prosecution motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I suppose you are aware as well that the Prosecution has now withdrawn their request in relation to -- in respect of one of the exhibits that they wanted to include. And that -- I'm referring to video -- to a particular video.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not aware of that. Of course I would have -- I would not have raised the issue had I been aware of it. Quite simply, we did not receive any such information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution no longer seeks to add one of the video -- I can give you the reference of the video. It's V00, or zero-zero - I wouldn't know if it's 0-0 or zero-zero - 3281. VOOO-3281. There are four other videos that are not being withdrawn. Do you have any further submissions, Mr. Wubben, or whoever will be dealing with this matter after the response of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the submissions of the Prosecution are laid out quite succinctly in our response. We do not seek to enter into evidence anything that as you termed grisly or that could be prejudicial. The Prosecution would like to point out that we are before a panel of professional Judges. We will see videos during this presentation of the case. We have already seen videos in the opening statements that showed rather touching and at times quite emotional footage and your Judges have to look at that as they would look at other videos. We would like to really emphasise the reason that the Prosecution felt that we should provide the entire videos is so that they could be seen in their context. And I think that what is quite clear in our response is that we have given the exact time slots on those videos that we think are relevant to a witness whom we will call a doctor who will be called to testify precisely to the type of work he has done within the region as it relates to exhumations and one of the persons that Mr. Oric is accused for being criminally responsible for. In that manner, we thought they were entirely relevant, that they would be probative, they corroborate the evidence of Mr. Stankovic. And I think that our ability to particularly point out now those segments of the video is an additional way in which the Defence can further prepare. We believe that they are relevant and therefore we would ask the Trial Chamber not to require that we withdraw them from our evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I reply just very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution has referred to seeing videotape, for example, in the opening speech which is -- which has a certain impact, emotional impact, let's say. Those are videotapes of Srebrenica at the time of the indictment directly relevant to the whole context of this case. The Prosecution is proposing to show videos of exhumations carried out in Croatia, another country, exhumations which have nothing to do with this case, and the Prosecution has clearly stated they are not exhumations related to any crimes in the indictment in order to prove to Dr. Stankovic has carried out exhumations. In our submission that is absolutely ridiculous. It really is ridiculous, as my colleague said, as showing videotapes of Dr. Gow of teaching. We accept he has carried out exhumations. Therefore, the reason for that evidence disappears. In our submission, there is no reason for having that evidence in, and it would set a bad precedent for it to be in, given its irrelevance. That's our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I thank learned counsel for his submissions. Certainly we will not burden this Trial Chamber with long videos of libraries of Dr. Gow's studies or students. But we would ask the Trial Chamber to please consider what, in essence, are prior statements of one of the witnesses who is coming forward, which is in essence seeing the witness perform the same functions professionally as we will offer the Trial Chamber that he performed in relationship to one of the victims in this indictment. We find that being totally relevant. This morning the Judges -- you have clearly explained to us that the policy is toward admitting evidence but also toward narrowing evidence that might contravene Rule 89(D). This does not, Your Honours. It is probative. And I would just fall back on our written submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we have heard enough on this. We will reserve our position and we will be handing a written decision on this motion which covers many other documents.
