It shouldn't take us much to decide this matter. I would expect that in the course of next week we should be in a position to hand down our position. It will cover, naturally, the 12 maps, the 28 videos, the three sets of photos -- not 28 videos, it's 27 now. And some other documents - I think they number 15 in all - identified through further investigation. We will also take into consideration the submissions that you made in your response, the other submissions, in relation to matters related to authenticity, provenance and all of that. That disposes of this motion. The Trial Chamber will decide it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Might I suggest to you, it's really coming back to some information that you had requested earlier. We have been able to contact the family of Mr. Bogicevic who has confirmed his death. Of course he was a well-known member of the community. They confirmed also that his death was in August of 2002 between the 4th and 5th of that year -- of that day. We will come back to you pertaining the number. Just to give you that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's a most important part. Thank you. I now come to the motion, which is again confidential, of the Prosecution filed on the 28th of September for protective measures for witnesses. So there are two persons, and I will be referring them as follows -- to them as follows: The first one is already coded and he is C001. The other one is named, but for the purposes of this hearing we will call him witness number 2, without mentioning his name. Who are you objecting that he or she be given protective measures that the Prosecution are asking for?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we object to C001. We are working on a motion now and we are going to hand it in by tomorrow at the latest. As for the other person, we do not oppose protective measures for this person, that is witness number 2. We shall present our reasons for that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the position that the Trial Chamber reserves is as follows: Instructing the stuff to prepare a decision in writing relating to the second person mentioned in the motion of the Prosecution, he is mentioned by name. We are deciding orally now that this person will be granted the protective measures of pseudonym, image, and voice distortion during the -- during this trial. However, since this person is mentioned by name in your motion, this oral decision will be followed by a written one which will be prepared by my staff and which we will sign either later on today or tomorrow or whenever. But you are advised that this person is being granted the protective measures sought. As regards Witness C001, we will wait for your motion and then we will see whether there are -- there is a reply from the Prosecution and we will decide accordingly. So this closes the matter on protective measures for witnesses. You should have received notice, if not the copy already, of a confidential ex parte Prosecution request for the issue of -- issuance of a subpoena in regard to a particular person that is mentioned in the ex parte part. I'm not going to ask you for any kind of a response for the time being. I don't know if you have received it or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have received that request. We are going to respond within the appropriate amount of time allocated to us for filing such a response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. It's not something that is urgent. I take it it can wait. It can wait. There are two other matters that arise from two other filings that occurred yesterday evening. One is the Prosecution's confidential notice of disclosure of declarations of Madam Racine Manas and additional witness statements dated 6th October 2004. I don't know if there are any remarks that the Defence have -- no. That's what I expected. The other may call for some kind of response on the part of the Defence. The other is the Prosecution's submissions substantiating selected disputed paragraphs of the Prosecution's pre-trial brief, also dated 6th October 2004. As you remember, this was provoked really by the Trial Chamber itself. There were some matters that you raised in your Defence pre-trial brief which, according to us, called for some kind of response. And the Prosecution has now graced us with their opinion on the matter. Do you want to make submissions or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are grateful to the Chamber for having raised the question. The Prosecutor filed his response. Anything that we would have to say now is for the trial stage, so we are going to respond to each and every one of these matters during the trial itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But at least you have the Prosecution's point of view and that's clear enough for your purposes at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I also want, before I move to the question of the length of the Prosecution case, I want to make sure that you have received the binder with the first -- with the statements of the first batch of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have received it. But I would kindly ask you to go back to another question. It seems to me that we haven't clarified it sufficiently. It has to do with Witness C004, or at least that's what I think you indicated, that we would discuss that today. Because on the 17th of September, 2004, the Prosecutor filed a request to postpone the discovery of the unredacted statement of Witness C004. We would just like to draw your attention now, the attention of the Trial Chamber now, to the possible consequences of this delayed discovery of the unredacted statement of this witness. I kindly ask the Trial Chamber to bear in mind the situation as it is. This witness does not speak only about Ratkovici, this witness talks about a series of attacks, perhaps I could say all the attacks that are relevant to the indictment. Also, this witness speaks about very important matters related to command responsibility and the possible responsibility of our client. This is to say that at the moment when we received this statement we have to carry out our own investigations, and we have to cross-examine practically all witnesses who are going to be called here during the trial. This could compel us to call back certain witnesses who perhaps gave their statements before we get this statement in its entirety. This statement is redacted to such a high degree that it says in one paragraph, for example, a person subordinate to my client, and I'm not going to say the name, says that he issued the order to attack and then the place of attack is redacted. This renders our investigations practically impossible. We need to have a fair trial and we need to have that principle observed. That is why I would like to request to have a decision to this effect passed as soon as possible because this could incur major expenses and costs for the Tribunal. We also had some correspondence with the Prosecutors and we asked for previously given statements to be handed over to us. The Prosecutor replied by saying that we should explain what we meant by this, namely that Rule 66(A)(ii] is quite clear; that was our answer. There is nothing for me to explain. These are statements that were given in different procedures. If we read the witness statements themselves very carefully, then it is quite clear that even on the basis of these statements there are indications that these witnesses talked to the authorities. Of course I'm not going to say here which particular authorities because I am trying to protect the witnesses. Also, we received other documents for -- from the Office of the Prosecutor, especially during the provisional release discussion. Could the Prosecutor please make an additional effort and give us these statements, too. For example, the statement of Witness C004. Could we have all these statements, rather, even in redacted form, but could we just have them please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who is going to address this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honours please, you will recall your very clear instruction that you issued at the pre-trial conference relating to disclosure matters generally; I recall it specifically. And Your Honours very usefully and hopefully indicated that all matters relating to disclosure should be put in writing. That happened and the Defence did indeed send us a letter after the pre-trial conference, and might I say that they made their position abundantly clear. Very clear. They initiated their letter dated the 1st of October using this phrase: "We are writing to inform you of the following items of disclosure which remain out" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: "... which remain outstanding." The Prosecution takes that to be a clear statement and takes at its face value that they were writing to inform us of indeed all the items of disclosure that remain outstanding. Now -- and then they enumerated a list of matters that they claim were -- remained outstanding, and the Prosecution has addressed those issues in a reply letter with the further disclosure of other material. Now, I can't indicate from looking at the transcript what precisely Madam Vidovic is talking about. I can say to you that the Prosecution will endeavour to provide anything that she is missing and could comply with our disclosure requirements and we have attempted to do this throughout. If Madam Vidovic is able to identify clearly to the Prosecution who precisely she is missing and requires by way of disclosure, then we will once again or disclose de novo materials. However, we have been following the procedure that your -- the Trial Chamber so helpfully pointed out, namely to deal with these issues in writing. And I can't say to you right now whether -- in fact, I can't identify precisely what Madam Vidovic is talking about. But we can and will provide anything that is clearly -- made clear to us, the nature of the material that is being sought. I can say that having received the letter of the 1st of October, 2004, in which the Defence set out all the items of disclosure which, and I'll quote again: "Remain outstanding," we have complied with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And with regard to Witness C004 and the question of delaying the disclosure, the Trial Chamber did -- we did our very best to make sure that the disclosure will not be delayed beyond the beginning of the trial. Unfortunately we could not do that. We need to verify certain matters ourselves, which we are doing, without which we are not really in the position to decide one way or another. I can't give details in a public hearing, but I suppose that very shortly we will have an update on the information that we are -- have asked for which would basically put us in the position to verify the facts on which the motion is predicated, is based. And after that, we should be in a position to decide. However, whichever way we decide and should we decide that the disclosure will be delayed until such-and-such a date, I can assure you, Madam Vidovic, that any measure you require to make good for that delayed disclosure will be met with. In other words, if it is necessary and the Trial Chamber is satisfied that it is necessary to bring back one or two or more or I don't know how many witnesses to testify further on particular matters, that request will be discussed, obviously, and if it is reasonable, it will be accepted. Whether the person would need to come here or whether the person could respond in some other fashion under Rule 92 bis, et cetera, that will be another matter. But for the time being, however much was our good intention to have this better decided before the beginning of the trial, we found ourselves in a predicament and we couldn't reasonably come to a conclusion without verifying certain facts, without which I believe we can't really come to a decision. But that should happen very soon, and the Prosecution and you should be able -- should be in a position to know whether there is going to be a disclosed -- a delayed disclosure in the first place. And if there is going to be a delayed disclosure, up to when. But we, ourself, don't know as to when.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just time for one matter. Earlier Your Honour referred to -- or Your Honour asked whether we had received a binder of the first batch of witnesses. I think I'm correct in stating - I haven't had time to confer with my colleague - but I don't think we received a batch of statements as such because we already had them presumably. So if that's the arrangement, then that's clear, we haven't received another binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When I said "binder," we want to make sure that you have been furnished, supplied with the statements of the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For you, it's different. For us it's a binder. We get a binder so I tend to refer to it as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. But what we would appreciate in that regard, Your Honours, is if we could receive a copy of the cover of the binder which is supplied to Your Honours so that we can keep track of which statements Your Honours have. Because when we come to cross-examine a witness it would be useful for us to know whether you have this past statement or that past statement. Otherwise we are in the dark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know actually if there is a -- I don't think there is even --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Or a schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because basically these are handed by the Prosecution not as a binder. We create the binder, our respective secretaries create the binder --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It just to keep track of which statements Your Honours have because it gets quite complicated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we go by name.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- statements. That's my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. We go by name. For example, if it is Witness C001 who is the first witness, he will have a separate binder and that will be Witness C001. If it's a short, very few -- it's not voluminous, we may include in that binder witness 2, witness 3, witness 4, but that's how we --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that's how we keep the records. At least far as I am concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Absolutely. Perhaps I wasn't entirely clear. We would appreciate from our side knowing that when a witness comes to be examined that Your Honours have, say, a statement from '92 and a statement from '94 so that we at least know from the start which statements you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That usually comes out in the course of the examination or the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because most of the time he is asked -- or she is -- the question is put to the witness: Did you give such statement, et cetera. And if we don't have it, I would immediately point out to the Prosecution that we don't have this statement. It has happened in the past. You always will have more than what we will have. I can assure you of that. Because you got disclosure of several documents that we don't get unless they are tendered in evidence. Otherwise we refuse them point-blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. It was simply a request to be kept in the loop as to what you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But that will be as we go along dealing with witnesses. You will realise what we have and what we don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the length of the case, Prosecution case. For the time being -- obviously for the time being I can't commit the Trial Chamber to the time which will be required for the Defence to -- Mr. Wubben, I know we discussed this before, and I'm going to -- I'm trying to bargain with you now, trying to squeeze the Prosecution a little bit further. Allowing for -- time for debating certain legal issues that necessarily have to arise from time to time, allowing for regular housekeeping time that is needed in the course of the trial, allowing for the time that you have already estimated you require for examination-in-chief, and roughly calculating the same time being needed by the Defence, may I ask you again to tell the Trial Chamber what is the maximum you anticipate is needed for the termination of the case, of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I refer to the list prepared by me and -- showing total number of hours of approximately 174 and adding what might probably and happy to know that 94 bis (C) turned out to be viva voce, then it should be around 180 hours. And in addition, it means around 11 weeks, 12 weeks. I should also refer to your remarks, Your Honour, when it comes to cross-examination, Defence counsel clearly stipulated 100 per cent or more and already showed some examples in which it might even be 200 per cent or 300 per cent. So -- anyhow, around 12 weeks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That allows also for time to debate legal or procedural issues that may arise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, when it comes to those debates I have no overview at this moment for any duration in time for legal issues. Defence counsel already made it clear that there will be legal issues, submissions, and your Trial Chamber is, from a practical point of view, focused on an expeditious trial. That means that from time to time we need some sessions for housekeeping indeed and that will support us as well. But that should be added of course to those weeks that I mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you have submissions on this except in regard to the time you think you require for cross-examination, which of course depends on the examination-in-chief. So...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, I would refer - Your Honour probably doesn't have it in front of you - to a letter which we wrote on the 30th of September, and it was copied to the senior legal officer of the Chambers. And I draw attention to that letter because from the Defence we are in the special position that if the estimate is wrong we're actually financially penalised. I don't think there's any secret about that. That's how the registry system works. So we have a particular concern in accurately predicting how long the trial will be. And our particular concern is that at least every item, that there be some calculation for each item, whether they are different -- there's a difference in estimates, that everything be taken into account. So in that letter, we point out that you have the Prosecution case, first of all, they have estimated their time for examination-in-chief, it's time for our cross-examination, obviously time for re-examination, time for questions by the Judges, motions. And then that's the estimate for the Prosecution case. Then of course we have the Defence case and we have all those categories again. We have Prosecution evidence in rebuttal, Defence evidence in rejoinder, and evidence ordered by the Chamber pursuant to Rule 98. Those are rule stages contemplated in the rules and we have no interest in drawing out the proceedings. We want to make ensure that there is a realistic assessment of all those stages. As far as cross-examination is concerned, Dr. Gow is an entirely special, separate category. He provides the whole background, the whole framework against which this case is to be seen. And as I said also, the Prosecution case will be -- the Prosecution examination-in-chief will be shorter because we are agreeing that he can be led for a large part of his evidence to save time. So it's certainly not the case that we're going to be taking 200, 300 per cent of the examination-in-chief. That's just Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have heard what -- the submissions of the parties. We are going to adopt an approach which will make it imperative, important, that each one of you will consider yourselves committed to this time limit. We will be -- we will move -- we will extend only if there are grave reasons, otherwise we are going to stick to this time limit that we are going to give. So basically pursuant to Rule 73 bis, if I remember well, of the Rules we come to the following determination: We are giving the Prosecution a total maximum of 26 weeks to complete the case. Basically this means 130 court days. The amount of time should include examination-in-chief, cross-examination by the Defence, and any re-examination. And almost needless to say, this has to include also time which may be required by each one of us who decide to put questions to witnesses, which we may decide to do from time to time, as well as housekeeping matters and possibly discussions of motions. This is why I am extending it from 24 weeks, that would have reflected what Mr. Wubben said, to 26 to allow for all contingencies and all possibilities. If we go -- if we miss the mark completely, then obviously we will need to revise the position. But I don't think if everyone sticks to the commitment we should find ourselves in that predicament.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I apologise, and I should have addressed it earlier, but it is beyond my own scope and it is your information in an earlier stage. There was a couple of weeks ago some information confirmed that in the month of November there might be two weeks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm coming to that. You will have noticed that I mentioned 26 weeks, and then I also mentioned court days, 130. And it's precisely because of what I am going to come up with. There will be, as we go along, the need to have interruptions, intervals, so that either you or the Defence will reorganise a little bit themselves, regroup. There may be the need to examine fresh information that comes along. So as is the practice in all the trials, there -- we may stop from time to time for a short time until this is dealt with. There will be a stop for sure in the beginning of November, a two-week break in the beginning of November. This is needed because time is needed for particularly the Trial Chamber to take stock of the amount of evidence that would have been brought forward in the meantime and also for you to revise a little bit the situation as it will obtain at the time. And then we should be able to reconvene immediately after. But please be prepared that there will be this stoppage in early November and that you should try to utilise the -- those two weeks as best as you can to then proceed -- be able to proceed with the trial in a more efficient manner. We will normally sit five days a week unless, as sometimes happens, things go wrong, and we will have to sit a day less, for example, if we finish with one witness and the other is not already here. But do plan for a five-day week. Do plan for a five-day week. You should schedule the arrival and departure of witnesses in the most economical way possible for the Tribunal. In other words, if a witness is going to begin giving the evidence on Wednesday of next week, there is no point in bringing that witness on the Tuesday of the week before or the Wednesday of the week before and keep that witness here for an entire week for briefing purposes and so on and so forth. So this I leave in your hands. I know that you have a policy that you adhere to. When we say that we will be allocating, for example, so many hours, so much time, for the Prosecution and for the Defence to -- it doesn't mean to say that we have to use all that time. If we can economise on that time and finish earlier, we'll try to finish earlier. In other words, there may be moments -- I mean, from what I can see so far, there may be witnesses coming forward who may be repeating events or -- events that others would have testified upon. If at any point in time we see that there is no such need to go through this -- these repetitions, we might call upon you, be it the Prosecution or the Defence, to cut short depending on what the matters are. But there are some matters, obviously, which appear on the face of it to be repetitions and we may interfere there. But I do want to appeal to you to economise on time as much as you can. As we see it, there will be a two-week break in the beginning of November. There will then be no further need for any breaks until the Christmas and New Year break. Before we come to the end of the Prosecution case, there will be Easter and there will be another break in Easter. As I see it, if we're still talking of 130 court days from today, taking into consideration the various breaks that we will have, this -- the Prosecution case will take us up to sometime in May of next year for completion. So this is what more or less we are envisaging at the present moment. Of course there will be -- if there is a need for further stoppages, et cetera, we will consider that, but only if it appears necessary to have further breaks. I do not exclude that these may come necessary either for you or for the Defence. These are very taxing and demanding trials, and sometimes situations are such that breaks are required. And then we'll try to compensate in some other way as we go along. Also our registrar -- our registrar will communicate with you in regard to the sittings in the week starting on the 18th and 19th of October, but this will be done later on. You will receive the information. I think there isn't much left. I think we can finish now unless there are any other issues that you would like to raise before we adjourn. Are there any remarks, comments, or anything that I may have missed completely that you would like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Madam Vidovic or Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have everything. I had another note here, but this has been dealt with. It's about outstanding disclosure matters. I think you -- the approach and the attitude from both of you is praiseworthy and it's very positive. So I think we can leave it at that. So we will adjourn until tomorrow, and tomorrow we are going to have the first witness. How long do you anticipate the first witness to last? Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, it depends, to a certain extent on the actual manner, the physical manner of producing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's your witness. If there is a witness who is really your witness, this is the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What I propose to do is to have the evidence in court, it's a selection of the Prosecution exhibits. We've accepted your invitation to put it in in staggered form, although I must say it's a large chunk of the Prosecution evidence. So what I propose to do is to take the witness through her annex and to describe the methods of obtaining the evidence and other relevant issues and then to tender the material as a whole having done that, having completed that aspect of her evidence. And then she'll be available for cross-examination. To get her to describe all of that and comment on various aspects of the material in her annex, and Your Honours will see it's the seizure details that's the really important part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's that part that I'm interested in and the Trial Chamber will be interested in. I'm hoping an hour and a half to two hours. I'm hoping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't gone through the file as yet, to be honest with you. I had it on my desk this morning, but I had to make choices. It was too much to read before I could even hope to start the sitting. I will take it home with me and go through it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's fairly simple material, if Your Honours please. It's basically methods that are adopted within the Tribunal -- within the OTP I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if you follow the system that we adopted in Brdjanin, for example, Mr. Inayet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I've read that transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Mr. Inayet came here on more than one occasion obviously because we were having the documents come in at intervals and some of them were obtained in the course of the trial itself. So they were new documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, the same will happen here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm hoping that will happen fairly quickly in the trial and that this whole exercise will be completed within a few weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And certainly by tomorrow's end of business you'll have the large -- the lion's share of the Prosecution material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very good. I think you're approaching it in a professional manner, and I think it should help us a lot in the beginning and at the end. That will also be very valuable for the Defence in at least seeing the parameters of -- within which you can then direct your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's perhaps a matter we can see tomorrow exactly how to proceed. We're not sure whether we'll be heard in our objections before the exhibits are admitted as well as having cross-examination. It's something which we can deal with tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We will deal with it tomorrow obviously. But the approach will be the following: We will not be discussing in front of the witness submissions. We will not be making submissions in the presence of the witness. I'm making that very clear. The witness is being brought here to give the Trial Chamber, and obviously to you as well, all the information that is available with regard to provenance, the way these documents were obtained and the way they were custodied before being brought here. Obviously if you have questions to put to the witness in relation to either the seizure or to the custody or whatever, I mean, you will have all the time you require to put those questions but not submissions. We will not be dealing with authenticity issues tomorrow. You can put questions related to authenticity, to provenance, and whatever, but not submissions in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. To take a concrete example, if the witness produces an exhibit for which there's, for example, let's say no information on provenance, our question is: Should we have our objections -- should we make our objection at that point during the examination-in-chief --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. In fact, what you are expected to do is the following, Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic: I would imagine -- if necessary, we will direct the proceeding to be as follows: The witness will be here and the Prosecution will be putting to the witness the various documents which the Prosecution intends to tender in evidence. I would imagine these are going to be categorised. For example, we may have a set of documents - I'm just imagining for the time being - that were obtained by investigator X from the police station in Vlasenica, for example. I'm just inventing an event. And you will hear what the witness has to say. If you want you can question the -- cross-examine the witness. And if you want to object to those documents, you can enter the objection then. I mean, you're expected to. You are also expected to say why you are objecting but not argue the case. The case will be argued later. Okay. The case will be argued -- in the course, for example, in other trials, some objections were entered in the beginning, and as we went along obviously it was no longer the case of keeping those objections. At the end of the trial we will revise -- I will call up on you, I will be keeping records of all these documents and when objections were made, if they had been withdrawn, if it is the case of having them withdrawn and so on, and then at the end of the trial before we adjourn for our deliberations, one of the things that we will deal with is which documents are still objected to. This is how I will be suggesting the two Judges to agree -- as a modus operandi. But this matter is visited in the beginning, it's visited in the end, and the decision of what will remain in or what will go out, we will take at the end of the day, after taking into consideration everything. But tomorrow, yes, you would be expected to say, yes, I object to this document because of this and because of that -- for example, because I contest the authenticity or I contest the provenance of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I understand there essentially will be three stages. During examination-in-chief we'll express an objection if we have one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll also cross-examine subsequently on the document, and subsequently we may also make separate submissions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But not in the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. Submissions I mean subsequent in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just one matter. I'm grateful to the Trial Chamber for the extra hints and guidelines on the procedure for tomorrow. But to just answer a matter Mr. Jones raised. He asked whether or not they would be required to cross-examine on pieces of evidence for which there is no evidence of provenance. What I propose to do - and you'll see it in the annex- is that some of the spaces are blank in -- those will not be tendered tomorrow. It's only where there is commentary by the author of the annex that the Prosecution will seek to tender into evidence the -- so there is something of provenance next to the item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And these are not matters that are arising the first in this trial. They have arisen in each and every trial, and there is an easy way to deal with them. I will be, together with Judge Brydensholt and Judge Eser, dealing with each document as it arrives. And our intervention will be limited as much as possible within the parameters of the guidelines we explained this morning. But what we certainly don't want is a debate on matters -- on issues of admissibility in the presence of tomorrow's witness. Obviously with other witnesses, if, for example, you are contesting all -- the authenticity of all documents supplied or given to the Tribunal by, I don't know which institute, I don't know which government, I don't know which person, which could be the case. Okay? At that point in time if tomorrow Racine Manas will say: This set of documents, from number 1 to number 20, were obtained from the security services centre of I don't know where, and you believe that that is not a reliable source, you will stand up and say: We object to the admission of these documents because we do not consider the source as a reliable one. And the matter ends there. You're not going to question the witness whether it's on the reliability of that source tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suppose, though, if -- obviously in the rules we're permitted to cross-examine on an area which may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But the thing is tomorrow's witness is not going to be the witness who will be in a position to guarantee the reliability of a source. What you can ask the witness is indeed whether she can confirm that the documents were obtained from that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And by whom and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But to clarify what the source is. For example, if we have information that the source is X, we can ask the witness what precisely is that source, can you clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we will not be debating tomorrow the reliability of that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I will only ask the witness what's within her knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But that's important. Then as we go along obviously we will have to refine this exercise. There will be witnesses to whom some of these documents will be referred and which may require you to cross-examine on several details and on reliability and all that, depending on who the witness is. I don't know. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I was just standing because I saw Your Honour looking at me and I thought you wanted me to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I looked at you because I saw you looking at me. That brings us to the end. We will reconvene tomorrow morning. I think, once more, you have shown a lot of cooperation in today's sitting which, as a result, we have been able to conclude -- to cover a lot of territory and also bring to a determination a lot of issues. I appreciate that and I'm saying this on behalf of the other two Judges, which I'm sure agree with me. Tomorrow we will start with the first witness and we'll reconvene at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of October, 2004 at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.41 p.m.,
